title: Redwood Edgecases Demo - long context / high TPS / streaming backpressure & timeouts
summary: Redwood AE/SE walked Nimbus through an edge-cases demo focused on long-context generation, high TPS load characteristics, and how streaming backpressure/timeouts surface and are mitigated in Redwood. Customer raised concerns about tail latency, retry semantics, and private deployment (VPC/KMS). Agreed to run a 48-hour high-TPS benchmark and share security docs and pricing.
next_steps: SE to share high-TPS benchmark plan and scripts (Ethan)
Send SOC2 + security whitepaper and KMS integration notes (Laura)
Schedule pilot kickoff and access to test cluster (Maya/Arjun)
Follow-up call to review benchmark results and cost projection in 1 week
action_items: Ethan Park - prepare and share benchmark scripts and load profile - 2026-07-17
Laura Kim - send SOC2 report, compliance slide deck, and KMS integration checklist - 2026-07-16
Maya Lopez - confirm pilot scope and internal stakeholders - 2026-07-18
header:
Date: 2026-07-15
Time: 14:30 - 15:25 UTC
Duration: 55 minutes
Location: Zoom
Recording: enabled
Attendees: Laura Kim (Redwood AE), Ethan Park (Redwood SE), Samir Rao (Redwood Product), Maya Lopez (Nimbus CTO), Arjun Patel (Nimbus Platform), Jenna Ortiz (Nimbus SRE), Chris Nguyen (Nimbus ML)
transcript:
[00:00] Laura Kim: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, we wanted to show you some real edge case behavior in the platform — long prompt contexts, high TPS, and what happens when streaming backpressure and timeouts occur.
[00:12] Maya Lopez: Thanks Laura. High level we care about two things: tail latency under load and correctness for very long contexts. We have chat history up to 100k tokens in some flows.
[00:25] Ethan Park: Got it. We'll demo the API, Console traces, and Redwood Optimize recommendations. Quick note, I'll be toggling between hosted and a simulated private config so you see routing differences.
[00:40] Arjun Patel: When you say 100k tokens, are you using KV cache or sharded context? Our current service is really sensitive to KV cache warmup.
[00:55] Ethan Park: Yeah, good call. For the demo I've got a pre-populated KV prefix cache to show warm vs cold behavior. We'll also show how batching and continuous caching reduces GPU work.
[01:12] Jenna Ortiz: And what about streaming backpressure? Our SREs saw client disconnects when we tried server push at 500 TPS.
[01:25] Laura Kim: Right, that's exactly one of the scenarios — streaming over HTTP/2 and server-sent events can hit backpressure if downstream can't keep up. We surface backpressure as stalled frames in the Console and we have queued retry/fallback logic in the routing layer.
[01:40] Chris Nguyen: Does that mean we get partial responses and then a retry? How does that affect tokens billed?
[01:50] Ethan Park: Good question. In hosted mode we attempt to resume streams and only re-render missing tokens; billing is per emitted token but we also have idempotency keys so you don't pay twice for the same completed response. There are corner cases with client timeouts where you might need a short reconciliation call.
[02:10] Maya Lopez: Can you show the Console trace for a streaming request that hit backpressure?
[02:18] Ethan Park: Sure, pulling up the Console now. (pause) Here you can see a live trace: request enters, routed to dedicated pool, continuous batching grouped these requests, then you see a spike in queue wait time at 00:27:10, and the stream stalls — Console annotates the stall and suggests actions.
[02:40] Ethan Park: Note the Console shows metrics: per-route latency p50/p95/p99, per-token throughput, and queued requests. Optimize will recommend reducing batch size or enabling prefix caching depending on workload.
[02:55] Arjun Patel: In practice, we'd probably want to failover to a lower-latency model to keep UX responsive. Is that an automated policy or manual?
[03:04] Samir Rao: Both — you can set an automated fallback policy: if p95 latency breaches X ms then route to a compatible variant (smaller quantized model) and log the event. You can also configure canary windows.
[03:20] Maya Lopez: Let's run a realistic script. Ethan, run the high-TPS profile.
[03:27] Ethan Park: Kicking off 1,000 concurrent vclients at T+0. Profile simulates mixed short/long contexts, about 60% short and 40% long (50k-100k token prefix). Starting...
[03:45] [05:00] (load generator running)
[05:05] Chris Nguyen: I'm seeing p95 climb immediately, p99 spikes to the multi-second range. What's the expected degradation?
[05:15] Ethan Park: So with long contexts we see more KV loads, bigger KV cache misses amplify per-request latency. Redwood's runtime tries to amortize kv-cache reads with continuous batching, but at extreme TPS the batch formation window increases latency unless you tune batching parameters.
[05:40] Laura Kim: Also, note the difference between cold and warmed cache. When I replay the same prefix the latency drops dramatically after cache warms.
[06:00] [08:00] (Console shows stream errors)
[08:05] Jenna Ortiz: We're getting these stream reset errors at roughly 1 in 500 requests. Is that retryable?
[08:15] Ethan Park: Yes, those are typically streaming timeouts or downstream disconnects. Our client-side SDK automatically retries streaming reads with exponential backoff; the server will try to resume where possible, otherwise we'll re-run the tail of generation on safe idempotency keys.
[08:32] Maya Lopez: How do you avoid double-generation costs in the resume path?
[08:38] Ethan Park: The idempotency key + server-side token cursor lets us avoid re-synthesizing tokens already acknowledged by the client. If a resume isn't possible we do a compensating cost reconciliation and flag the request in billing logs for review.
[08:55] Arjun Patel: Can I see the raw request and response headers for one of the failed streams?
[09:02] Ethan Park: Yep, here in the Console trace — headers show x-redwood-id, idempotency-key, client-timeout-ms, and we log the kernel fallback used. You can download the full HAR for a session.
[09:20] [12:00] (demo: switch to Private config)
[12:10] Laura Kim: Switching to a simulated private/VPC environment — same model, different routing: private control plane, customer VPC peering. Here you'll notice TLS termination happens in your VPC and logs are forwarded to your SIEM via the Kinesis hook.
[12:32] Maya Lopez: For compliance we need KMS integration and audit logs for model access. How mature is that?
[12:40] Samir Rao: We support customer-managed keys via KMS/HSM and maintain audit trails per invocation. We can configure retention, and we support SAML SSO and RBAC to limit who can trigger sensitive workflows.
[12:58] Jenna Ortiz: Does Private change latency? The peering adds a hop.
[13:06] Ethan Park: There's small network overhead, but because inference happens in the same region and we avoid public egress it can actually help tail latency for some customers. The bigger gains are deterministic routing and data residency.
[13:25] Chris Nguyen: Back to streaming: what's the recommended client-side pattern to handle partial responses?
[13:33] Ethan Park: Use the SDK's streaming iterator, respect backpressure signals (pause reading), and use idempotency keys for resume. If you can't resume, fall back to polling or a short synchronous call to get the final tokens. We have example code in the docs and the SDK.
[13:55] Maya Lopez: Show us an Optimize run for this workload.
[14:00] Ethan Park: Opening Redwood Optimize. It ingests workload traces and suggests: enable prefix caching for 40% long context workload, set batch_max_tokens to Y, reduce batching window from 20ms to 8ms under high TPS, and recommend a quantized variant for automated fallback.
[14:22] Laura Kim: Optimize also projects cost savings if you adopt caching + smaller fallback models. Here you can see a per-token cost delta.
[14:35] Arjun Patel: We need confidence that fallback doesn't lead to unacceptable quality regressions. Can we run A/B on queries?
[14:42] Samir Rao: Absolutely. We support canary rollouts and A/B evaluation bundles. Optimize can produce eval sets and track quality regressions automatically.
[14:55] [20:00] (load sustained, queue growth)
[20:05] Chris Nguyen: We're seeing a period where queue wait times hit 300ms for many requests and the streaming responses are being chunked smaller. Some clients drop.
[20:20] Ethan Park: That's the backpressure curve — when consumers can't keep up we have two levers: reduce batch window to prioritize latency, or drop to a capacity tier that favors lower latency at higher cost. You can set automatic rules to do either.
[20:40] Maya Lopez: What's the SLA behavior for dedicated pools under those conditions?
[20:46] Laura Kim: For Dedicated, we provide capacity guarantees and SLOs. If you hit sustained overload we can route to burst capacity or scale more nodes per your reserved commit; in Private we can also escalate to manual autoscale triggers.
[21:05] Jenna Ortiz: For billing, if we switch to a higher-cost fallback mid-request, how does the invoice reflect that?
[21:12] Ethan Park: We break down cost by route and by model variant; Optimize shows per-request cost attribution and you'll see the fallback usage as a separate line item. We can also tag requests with customer business unit for chargeback.
[21:30] [26:00] (demo: simulate client timeouts and reconnects)
[26:10] Ethan Park: I'm going to simulate a client abort at 1500ms and trigger reconnect. Watch the Console: stream stalls, reconnect attempts, resume attempt, then a final re-run for the last 200 tokens because the resume cursor couldn't reconcile after a network reset.
[26:35] Chris Nguyen: That re-run produced duplicate tokens in one case we saw earlier. How do you detect duplicates?
[26:42] Ethan Park: We insert token sequence checksums in the trace and the SDK validates them on resume. Duplicate detection is best-effort in a few pathological network partitions. We surface those cases to a flagged list for you to inspect.
[27:00] Maya Lopez: Could we avoid that by increasing client read timeouts?
[27:05] Ethan Park: Yes, increasing client read timeout reduces premature disconnects, but it can increase tail latency from the user's perspective. That's the UX tradeoff. Optimize can simulate the tradeoff and recommend client timeout knobs.
[27:25] [33:00] (discussion: long context memory and storage cost)
[33:05] Arjun Patel: For 100k token contexts, what's the storage/IO hit and how does Redwood mitigate it?
[33:12] Samir Rao: We store prefixes in a KV store optimized for low latency access and employ compression + sharding. We also recommend summarization or selective prefixing in Optimize to reduce IO. There's a cost/quality tradeoff.
[33:30] Maya Lopez: Do you support on-the-fly prefix eviction policies?
[33:35] Ethan Park: Yes, you can configure TTLs and LRU policies; Optimize will suggest good defaults based on access patterns.
[33:50] [40:00] (customer questions: security & compliance)
[40:05] Jenna Ortiz: We need clarity on auditability: who invoked what model and with which prompt, retention windows, and key rotation.
[40:12] Samir Rao: Audit logs include invocation ID, user, model, and truncated prompt hash. Retention is configurable and we can support SOC2/ISO requirements. Key rotation is via your KMS.
[40:30] Maya Lopez: Can you provide a sample retention policy and audit-log export?
[40:35] Laura Kim: I'll attach the sample policy and export template in the follow-up email.
[40:42] Arjun Patel: If we do a pilot, we want a 48-hour full-load run with both cold and warm cache. Can Redwood run that or do you need us to provide load?
[40:52] Ethan Park: We can run it with our benchmark harness but we'll need network egress access to your test VPC and an idempotent dataset. We'll share scripts and CloudWatch/Prometheus collectors.
[41:10] Maya Lopez: Ok let's set that as next step.
[41:15] [48:00] (wrap-up and recaps)
[48:05] Laura Kim: Quick recap: we'll share the SOC2 and KMS docs, Ethan will share benchmark scripts and run the 48-hour high-TPS test, and we'll schedule a follow-up to review results and cost impact.
[48:20] Maya Lopez: Sounds good. Also please include a sample SDK retry config and the Optimize projection for cost.
[48:30] Laura Kim: Noted. Anything else?
[48:35] Chris Nguyen: One more ask: can you surface kernel-level logs when we hit stalls so we can triage performance regressions?
[48:42] Samir Rao: We can expose more detailed runtime traces under an NDA — we'll include the request in the follow-up and escalate to Eng if needed.
[48:55] Maya Lopez: Great. Thanks everyone.
[49:00] Laura Kim: Thanks all. We'll follow up with the artifacts and docs.
[54:30] (meeting ends)
